newsitem.title: Israel: Israeli-Palestinian talks on Hebron begin.
newsitem.headline: Israeli-Palestinian talks on Hebron begin.

text.p: Israelis and Palestinians opened formal talks on Monday on a long-delayed Israeli troop redeployment in the West Bank city of Hebron, with the United States warning that swift progress was vital.

Israeli and Palestinian negotiators, who agreed on an agenda for talks on Sunday, met at Erez crossing between Israel and the Gaza Strip for a closed session to begin the tough bargaining over Israeli demands for better security for 400 militant Jewish settlers in the heart of the city of 100,000 Arabs.

U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher, spending a day in Israel to underline Washington's efforts to resume peace talks after violence that took 74 lives, urged a quick resolution of the dispute over the Israeli pullback in Hebron, already delayed by nearly seven months.
"I think we also have an acute sense of the shortness of time and desire that we make progress as rapidly as possible," Christopher told reporters.
Christopher said he was reassured Netanyahu did not want to "rescind or modify" the agreement reached by the government he unseated in last May's election.
But he shared Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's view that security provisions had to be changed after the recent fighting in which 15 Israelis and 59 Palestinians died.
"Within the implementation, practical questions arise and I think it's only fair to say that those practical questions now involve the recent violence," Christopher said.

Despite the U.S. call for urgency, there were likely to be deep differences over terms for redeployment, seen by Palestinians since Netanyahu took office as a test of his commitment to the peace process.

"In the framework of the understandings of the agreement, we are working -- as is our right -- to achieve the requested arrangements to anchor security and to have redeployment in Hebron in more secure conditions," Netanyahu told parliament.

"We are preparing to implement the redeployment in Hebron while guarding two basic principles: securing the lives, existence and security of residents of the Jewish commmunity in Hebron...(and) protecting our holy places in Hebron," he said.
But Palestinians oppose anything beyond minor changes to their agreement with the previous Israeli government on moving troops out of much of the Arab city.

"They want to modify the Hebron agreement in a way which will bring about a complete change of the agreement," said a Palestinian official. "We refuse to change the agreement or modify it, but we will accept only simple additions to the agreement that will not change the basis of the Hebron agreement."

Netanyahu's policies, which have thrown the five-year-old Arab-Israeli peace process into disarray, drew a scathing attack in parliament from former prime minister Shimon Peres, the Labour Party leader Netanyahu defeated in May.

Peres, who negotiated the unimplemented agreement on Hebron, listed Netanyahu's "ridiculous actions" since taking office, primarily the opening of a new entrance to an archaeological tunnel near Moslem holy sites in Jerusalem last month that triggered the violence.
"In these 111 days Israel lost a lot of goodwill in the entire world, including in the United States of America," he said. "In these 111 days, the amount of blood spilled was not small."
